title: The Fee You Never Repriced: What Rising Payment Costs Are Quietly Taking Off Every Sale
excerpt: Spring revenue is climbing into the Christmas trading peak, and so is the quiet cost of simply getting paid. Here's why most owner-led businesses haven't repriced for it.
content:
Spring trading is in full swing, and most owner-led businesses along the East Coast are now locking in Christmas stock orders, casual rosters and the marketing spend that carries them through the final quarter. Revenue is about to climb. For a lot of businesses, so is the number of transactions running through the till, the online checkout and the invoice portal every single day.

What rarely gets a second look in all of that planning is the cost of actually getting paid. Most businesses set their card surcharge, chose their payment gateway or signed up for a buy now pay later provider years ago, priced it in once, and never revisited it since. In that time, the cost of accepting a card has crept up, buy now pay later has become a normal part of how customers pay, and the share of sales running through the more expensive payment methods has quietly grown.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led businesses heading into their busiest quarter is that revenue rises at the same time the average cost of collecting that revenue rises too, and because both movements happen gradually, neither shows up as a single alarming number on the profit and loss. It shows up later, as a margin that stops tracking the sales line the way it used to.

Why Payment Costs Hide Inside a Line Called "Bank Fees"

Most charts of accounts bury the entire cost of accepting payment inside one bank fees or merchant fees line, treated as a fixed monthly overhead rather than a cost that moves directly with revenue. That makes it easy to miss as a variable cost. When sales rise, owners expect that line to rise roughly in step, and rarely check whether the underlying rate has also crept up, which compounds the effect inside a figure that already looks unremarkable. For a business turning over a meaningful volume of card and buy now pay later sales each year, even a small lift in the blended rate is a real dollar figure sitting quietly inside a cost line nobody reviews, and it rarely gets questioned because the bookkeeper reconciling that line is doing exactly what they should be doing, which is matching the bank statement, not auditing whether the rate behind it has moved.

Every New Way to Pay Is a Different Margin Decision

Tap and go, PayID, bank transfer and the various buy now pay later providers each carry a different cost structure, and a standard card transaction is rarely the most expensive option on offer. Buy now pay later in particular is often priced at a multiple of what a standard card transaction costs the business, not the customer. Every time a new payment option is added for convenience, it is really a pricing decision, even though it rarely gets signed off as one. As the share of sales running through the costlier options grows over the gift-buying months, the average cost of acceptance rises precisely when sales volume, and therefore transaction count, is at its highest for the year. A business that quietly let its buy now pay later share grow from a small fraction of sales to a third of them has effectively repriced itself downward without a single conversation about it.

What a Repricing Conversation Actually Looks Like

The fix is not to ban convenient payment methods. It starts with pulling twelve months of settlement reports by payment type and working out the true blended cost of acceptance as a percentage of revenue, then comparing that figure to whatever rate was last used to set prices or surcharges. From there it is a deliberate choice: pass the cost through as a surcharge, build it into the headline price, or absorb it on purpose with full visibility of what that costs across a year. That is exactly the kind of line-by-line review a Cost & Margin Deep Dive is built to produce, ranking where the dollars are actually leaking rather than guessing at it from the bank statement. For a trades business in regional Queensland taking card payments on-site, or an online retailer processing a national spike in buy now pay later orders through November and December, the number is different, but the exercise is the same.

For businesses across the East Coast heading into their busiest trading months, the answer is rarely a one-off fix. It is having someone who checks that number every quarter as a matter of course, the kind of ongoing financial oversight a fractional CFO partnership is built around, rather than revisiting it only when the merchant account was first set up and never again.

faqs.q: How much do payment processing fees typically cost an Australian SME?
faqs.a: It varies by payment mix, but the pattern we see is that a blended rate across card, tap and go and buy now pay later is almost always higher than owners expect, because buy now pay later in particular tends to cost several times more than a standard card transaction. The only way to know your own number is to pull the settlement reports and calculate it directly rather than estimate it.

faqs.q: Should my business pass on card surcharges or absorb the cost?
faqs.a: There is no universal right answer, and it depends on your customer base, your margin and your competitors' approach. What matters more is that the decision is made deliberately with the real blended cost in front of you, rather than inherited from whatever was set up when the merchant account was first opened. A current view of your own pricing structure is the right starting point before deciding either way.

faqs.q: Why do buy now pay later fees affect my profit margin so much?
faqs.a: Buy now pay later providers typically charge the business a fee well above a standard card transaction in exchange for taking on the customer's repayment risk and handling collection. As more customers choose that option, especially during gift-buying months, the average cost of every sale rises even though nothing about your pricing or your costs of goods has changed.

faqs.q: How often should I review my merchant and payment provider agreements?
faqs.a: Annually at a minimum, and ideally every six months if your payment mix is shifting quickly. Interchange rates and buy now pay later terms change more often than most businesses expect, and a provider that was competitive two years ago is not guaranteed to still be the cheapest option for your current transaction volume and mix.

faqs.q: Does offering more ways to pay actually help profitability?
faqs.a: It can help conversion and average order value, particularly for larger purchases, but that upside needs to be weighed against the extra cost of acceptance, not assumed to be free. The businesses that get the most benefit are the ones that track the trade-off deliberately, building that review into a regular cash flow discipline rather than treating it as a set-and-forget decision.

faqs.q: What's the easiest way to find my true cost of accepting payment?
faqs.a: Export twelve months of settlement reports from your payment providers, broken down by payment type, and divide total fees by total revenue processed through each method. That blended percentage, compared against whenever your prices or surcharges were last set, usually reveals the gap in minutes rather than requiring a major project.
